  "text": "Every winter, the village hired someone to count the houses.

It was easy work, my uncle said. Start at the church, follow the road, stop at the bridge. Never count after dark.

There were forty-three houses in November.

In December, there were forty-four.

The extra house stood between the bakery and the school, narrow and yellow, with a bicycle leaning against its fence. Nobody answered when I knocked.

“Forty-three,” my uncle said, correcting my report.

“You haven't looked.”

“I used to do your job.”

That night, someone left a photograph beneath my door. It showed me on the yellow house's steps, holding a birthday cake. I was perhaps seven. A woman's hand rested on my shoulder.

I recognized the cake. My mother had dropped it the year before she died. We ate the undamaged half straight from the kitchen floor.

In the photograph, it was whole.

I went back at dusk.

Through the window, I saw a table set for two. A woman stood at the sink, her sleeves rolled above her elbows.

Without turning, she lifted one finger: wait.

My uncle found me at the gate.

“She'll finish washing up,” he said. “Then she'll remember something in the oven. Then she'll need you to fetch a plate.”

The woman dried her hands.

“How do you know?”

He pulled me toward the road. Behind us, a cupboard opened.

At the bridge, he finally stopped.

For years, I had wondered why he wore a watch that didn't work.

Now he showed me its face.

Behind the glass, the second hand was still moving backward."
